name: Ceramides
lead: Ceramides are skin-identical waxy lipids that are added to moisturizers, cleansers and supplements to restore the skin's barrier. People use them to keep skin smooth, hydrated and calm, including while using drying treatments such as retinoids or acne products, which supports the clear, even, comfortable-looking skin that is the usual goal of a skincare routine.

Ceramides are a family of waxy lipid molecules, each made of a sphingosine base joined to a fatty acid by an amide bond. They are found in the membranes of eukaryotic cells, take part in cell signaling such as differentiation, proliferation and programmed cell death, and are a component of vernix caseosa, the waxy coating on newborn skin [1].

In the outer skin layer (stratum corneum), ceramides are the major lipid constituent of the lamellar sheets in the spaces between cells, which are thought to provide the epidermal barrier. The intercellular lipid domain is generally described as containing roughly equimolar amounts of free fatty acids, cholesterol and ceramides [2][3]. Moisturizers that contain ceramides, often with cholesterol and fatty acids, are marketed for dry skin, eczema-prone skin and barrier repair.

A 2025 review describes ceramide as a thoroughly studied skincare compound used medically to repair barrier defects in conditions such as atopic dermatitis and dry skin [4]. A systematic review and meta-analysis has compared ceramide-containing moisturizers with other moisturizers in atopic dermatitis [5]. Ceramides also appear in a separate metabolic literature, where particular circulating ceramides are studied as lipotoxic mediators and risk markers, which is unrelated to topical use [6][7].

paras: Ceramides are waxy lipids made of sphingosine joined to a fatty acid by an amide bond; the name derives from the Latin cera, wax. [1] In the stratum corneum, the skin's outermost layer, they sit with cholesterol and free fatty acids in the lipid matrix around the corneocytes, often described as 'bricks and mortar'. [1][3]

This matrix forms a water-impermeable barrier that limits evaporative water loss and helps keep microbes out. A typical epidermal lipid mix is roughly equimolar, with ceramides around 50 percent by weight. [1] Dry or polluted air, harsh sulfates, heat, UV exposure and ageing are reported to lower skin ceramide levels, which is the basis for adding them back through moisturisers. [1][2]
Epidermal ceramides come in many classes (such as NS, NP, AP and EOS) that differ in their sphingoid base and fatty acid chain, and ratios shift in inflamed skin such as psoriasis. [1]

The stratum corneum is the outermost epidermal layer, about 15 to 20 layers of flattened dead cells called corneocytes embedded in the lipid matrix, roughly 10 to 40 micrometres thick depending on body site, with cells moving from the basal layer to the surface in about two weeks before shedding. [23] Ceramides also form a layer that replaces the cell membrane during cornification and bonds to the cornified envelope, supporting the barrier. [23] In psoriasis, AS and NS ceramides rise while EOS, AP and NP fall, which may weaken the water barrier. [1]

sections.h: How ceramides are used to improve appearance
paras: Skin that is dry or has a weakened barrier looks rough, flaky, dull and reactive, and can sting or redden with active ingredients. Ceramide moisturizers aim to replace barrier lipids so the surface looks smoother and tolerates treatment better. A typical use is as the moisturizing step after cleansing, often alongside niacinamide, hyaluronic acid or sunscreen, and as a buffer for retinoid or exfoliant use.[8][27]

Brands commonly pair ceramides with cholesterol and fatty acids, reflecting the roughly 1:1:1 molar ratio of the three lipids found in skin, which Peter Elias's review says are all needed to form the lamellar structures that regulate barrier function.[29] Some products use lab-made 'pseudo-ceramides' because natural ceramides are costly to extract and hard to keep stable, according to a Dazed report on the Curel brand.[28]

The skin's lipid barrier was worked out over several decades. Until the 1960s the barrier was often thought to sit in the granular layer rather than the stratum corneum; later lamellar lipid work, including Elias and Friend's 1975 description of an expanded lipid domain around corneocytes, established the idea of an epidermal permeability barrier.[29] Reviews credit work from the 1970s to 1990s with showing that the intercellular lipids are an equimolar mixture of ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids and that all three are needed for the barrier.[29][2]

Ceramide-containing skincare then moved from dermatology into consumer products. CeraVe launched in the United States in 2005 with dermatologist input, was acquired by L'Oreal in 2017 as part of a deal reported at $1.3 billion, and became one of the fastest-growing skincare brands in 2020, helped by YouTuber Hyram Yarbro's promotion.[25][26] A Super Bowl advertisement in 2024 featured actor Michael Cera.[25]

During the 2020 lockdowns many people layered retinol, acids and strong exfoliants at home; brands and dermatologists reported more irritation, acne, rosacea and perioral dermatitis, and responded with 'barrier repair' lines.[28] Glossy reported in March 2022 that #skinbarrier had 302 million TikTok views, #ceramides 104 million and #cerave 1.6 billion, with dermatologist influencers credited for spreading the message.[27]

Industry figures quoted in the trade press described ceramides as 'synonymous with skin barrier health' and said consumers had been encouraged to overuse actives; dermatologist Josh Zeichner compared the barrier to tiles held together by grout made of ceramides, fatty acids and cholesterol.[27] Brand-affiliated experts are among those quoted, and the Nylon report presents CeraVe's claim that all its products share a blend of three ceramides as the company's own statement.[26]

In appearance communities ceramide creams are discussed as inexpensive basics for the skin routine, usually described alongside gentle cleansers, sunscreen, and retinoids or acne treatments rather than as a stand-alone intervention. Drugstore availability, large pack sizes and low prices are frequently cited reasons for the popularity of the CeraVe range.[26]

Ceramide-containing creams, lotions and cleansers are used to ease dryness and support the skin barrier, including in people using drying acne or retinoid treatments. A 2024 split-face randomized trial examined a ceramide and niacinamide moisturizer versus a hydrophilic cream alongside topical anti-acne treatment in mild to moderate acne [8].
Oral products are also sold: a registered study examined rice ceramide supplementation and skin health, and another tested a hair, skin and nails supplement [9][10].

Ceramide-containing emollients are used in atopic dermatitis and dry skin, where barrier lipids are reduced; a study of stratum corneum in atopic dermatitis analyzed ceramide content per unit mass, and a 2024 review examined a pseudo-ceramide and eucalyptus extract moisturizer in atopic dermatitis [4][5][11]. Reviews of ichthyosis vulgaris describe a barrier made fragile and permeable by filaggrin loss [12].

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Indian Journal of Dermatology compared ceramide-containing moisturizers with other moisturizers in atopic dermatitis [5]. A registered study compared the skin barrier repair function of two ceramide-containing moisturizers (CeraVe lotion) in 30 participants [13]. The 2025 review summarizes established benefits as moisture barrier creation, hydration, pH regulation, inflammation control and improved skin function and appearance [4].

Ceramides are marketed in moisturisers, cleansers, serums, sunscreens and hair products, with the barrier claim at the centre of brand messaging; Wikipedia lists soaps, shampoos, skin creams and sunscreens among cosmetics that may contain them, and some eczema medications include them as a complement to treatment. [1] Ceramides are discussed in skincare circles alongside niacinamide and retinoids, since barrier-supporting moisturisers are used with drying actives. [8]
Supplements marketed as oral ceramides, often from rice or other plants, are sold for skin hydration. [9]

No systemic risks from topical ceramides in skin-care formulations have been reported. The metabolic literature associates elevated circulating ceramides with insulin resistance, fatty liver and cardiovascular risk markers, but that concerns endogenous lipids in tissues and blood rather than moisturizer use [6][7][14].

The skin barrier lies mainly in the stratum corneum, built of protein-rich corneocytes and lipid-rich intercellular domains, and prevents loss of water and solutes while blocking pathogens and irritants [3]. Ceramides are structurally diverse, with chain length, hydroxylation and saturation differing among species, and are central to the lamellar organization [2].

In cells, ceramide is formed by three pathways: breakdown of sphingomyelin, de novo synthesis starting from palmitate and serine in the endoplasmic reticulum, and a salvage pathway that reuses sphingosine [1]. Ceramide also acts in signaling, for example in exosome formation and apoptosis, which is studied separately from skin care [1].

Ceramides are studied in metabolism as lipotoxic mediators [6], in insulin resistance [7], as plasma markers [14] and across many ceramide species [15]. Registered studies examine ceramide-based nanoliposomes in cancer, serum ceramides in lupus and myocardial infarction, and plasma ceramides and vascular function [16][17][18][19][20]. A phase 2 study tested a ceramide cream in women with cutaneous breast cancer [21].

Beyond the skin, ceramides were once seen as purely structural membrane components but are now known to act as signalling molecules regulating differentiation, proliferation and programmed cell death. [1] Elevated circulating ceramides are linked in research to insulin resistance, fatty liver and cardiovascular events, which is a separate field from cosmetic use. [1][6][14]

Human research on topical ceramides includes a 2023 meta-analysis of ceramide-containing moisturizers in atopic dermatitis [5], a 2024 randomized split-face trial of a ceramide and niacinamide moisturizer in acne [8], and a registered comparison of two ceramide-containing moisturizers for barrier repair [13]. Other registered work covers oral rice ceramide and a nourishing supplement [9][10], and serum ceramide measurement as a biomarker in lupus, myocardial infarction and vascular disease [17][18][19].

Ceramide-based injectable or infused therapeutics are in early cancer trials (a phase 1 nanoliposome study in acute myeloid leukemia and another in advanced solid tumors) and are unrelated to cosmetic use [16][22].

DermNet New Zealand groups moisturiser ingredients into emollients that soften skin, occlusives such as petrolatum and dimethicone that reduce water loss, and humectants such as glycerine and urea that draw water into the outer layer; it describes moisturisers as reducing dryness, improving barrier function, and in eczema helping control mild disease and reducing flare severity and steroid needs. It lists irritation, contact allergy to fragrances or preservatives, and acne-prone skin flare with occlusives as risks. [24] That page does not cover ceramides specifically.

timeline.event: Elias and Friend describe the expanded lamellar lipid domain around corneocytes, a basis for the permeability barrier concept.[29]
Research shows ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids are all required for barrier lamellae.[29]
Cosmetic Ingredient Review publishes a safety assessment of ceramides used in cosmetics.[1]
Lockdown skincare boom and CeraVe social media growth.[25][26]
Barrier-repair lines proliferate; #skinbarrier reaches about 302 million TikTok views.[27][28]
Meta-analysis of ceramide moisturizers in atopic dermatitis published.[5]
Split-face trial of ceramide and niacinamide moisturizer in acne published; CeraVe Super Bowl advertisement.[8][25]

lore.intro: Ceramides are discussed mainly through skincare and 'skin barrier' content on TikTok and in beauty media, and as a staple ingredient in drugstore routines.[26][27]

claims.claim: Ceramide moisturizers repair a damaged skin barrier.
claims.believers: Brands and derm-influencers present ceramides as the core ingredient of barrier repair, with #ceramides at 104 million TikTok views by 2022.[27]
claims.experts: Reviews describe ceramides as a major lipid of the barrier and a thoroughly studied skincare ingredient used in atopic dermatitis and dry skin; a 2023 meta-analysis compared ceramide moisturizers with other moisturizers in atopic dermatitis.[2][4][5]

claims.claim: Over-exfoliating and stacking actives breaks the barrier, and ceramides help recovery.
claims.believers: Beauty-brand founders quoted in 2022 said consumers broke their barriers with quick fixes.[27][28]
claims.experts: A 2024 split-face trial examined a ceramide and niacinamide moisturizer alongside anti-acne treatment, and dermatologists in the press link barrier problems to overuse of actives.[8][28]

claims.claim: Any product that lists ceramides is a true barrier moisturizer.
claims.believers: Front-label ceramide claims are central to brand messaging.[1]
claims.experts: Dermatology commentary notes that formulation, not the label claim alone, determines performance; reviews of moisturizer composition describe emollient, occlusive and humectant roles.[24]

claims.claim: Oral ceramide supplements improve skin hydration.
claims.believers: Rice and plant ceramide supplements are marketed for skin hydration.[9]
claims.experts: Registered studies have examined rice ceramide and a hair, skin and nails supplement.[9][10]

claims.believers: A Curel-affiliated dermatologist said ceramides may help prevent superficial ageing.[28]
claims.experts: A 2025 review lists hydration, pH regulation, inflammation control and improved skin appearance among established ceramide benefits, and Wikipedia notes that ageing lowers skin ceramide levels.[1][4]

claims.claim: CeraVe's three-ceramide blend is what makes it work.
claims.believers: CeraVe says all its products share the same three-ceramide blend that repairs the barrier.[26]
claims.experts: The claim is the company's; a registered study compared barrier repair of two ceramide-containing CeraVe moisturizers in 30 participants.[13][26]
